"Friend" may be a bit strong. "Good acquaintances" probably describes things better. We are both acoustic musicians, but don't share a lot of other interests. He can play only a little because of his illness, and indeed can only talk for a limited time at a time. I don't want to burden him with heavy conversation, but I'd like to think I could make my visits good. What would you suggest? (He detests commiseration, which I quite understand)
A friend is dying. We are both middle-aged men. Voaters, what do you think we might talk about?
Anything but the thing killing him. Be the reprieve, discuss old times, funny memories or current events. Tell him about your day if he hasn't the energy to discuss his.
Both of us are on board with that.
May have him help you write something. Knowing that a little creative piece of you will live one can make someone feel better.

The joy of life, and the fear of death. Don't be afraid to talk about "heavy stuff". Everybody, including him, might be afraid to talk about how much dieing sucks, or how terrible some things in everybody's life are, but I believe that talking about it is more likely to take some of the burden from his heart rather than add to it.

If I were in his shoes I'd want people to just talk to me about regular things - books, movies, ideas. Especially if you're more acquaintances than close friends. I think being there to just provide some company and a reprieve from facing the inevitably of his death is a great thing you can do.

I was recently in the hospital. My doctors and nurses didn't think I would make it. (Cancer. Infections.) That lasted for over two months.

I was stuck in my hospital bed too feeble to move much. I loved hearing about what was going on in the world outside my little room and hearing about what friends and family were up to... My family brought in music to listen to. Sometimes they would talk to each other and I could relax and listen.

The biggest thing was not being alone. Even when I got home, it was easy to feel isolated. Having someone just be in the room with me was a big deal, even if they were just reading a book.

I guess that's the point I'm trying to make. Being there is the important thing.
